header.title: Two-Step Compound Events
header.subtitle: List every outcome, then count: lists and arrays

meta.lesson-focus: Use lists and arrays to record outcomes of two-step compound experiments — the Heads and Tails game, drawing two team leaders from a class; calculate probabilities by counting favourable outcomes over total outcomes.
meta.ac9-descriptor-text: list all outcomes for compound events both with and without replacement, using lists, tree diagrams, tables or arrays; assign probabilities to outcomes
meta.sa-conceptual-understanding: The likelihood of an event occurring can be affected by another event that has already taken place

html.section0_intro: Last year you found the probability of a single event. Today an experiment has two steps. These three questions check the one-step skills you need.
html.section_warmup:
A real situation that is secretly today's probability.

Your class runs a Heads and Tails stall at the school fair. A player pays $2, flips two coins, and wins $5 if both land heads.

Someone says: “There are three results: two heads, one head, no heads. So you win one game in three and the stall loses money.” Is that right? Before you set the prices you need to know the real chance of two heads.

Flipping two coins is a compound event: two steps, one after the other. Today you list every outcome with a systematic list or an array, then find a probability by counting: favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes.

html.section3_desc: Two fair coins are flipped. Drag each event into P = ¼ or P = ½. Use the four outcomes HH, HT, TH, TT.
html.sort_activity:
Sort each two-coin event by its probability
Two heads Exactly one head Two tails First coin is heads Head first, then tail (HT) Both coins land the same Tail first, then head (TH) Second coin is tails

P = ¼ (1 outcome of 4)

P = ½ (2 outcomes of 4)

💡 HT and TH are different outcomes: the first coin is different. That is why “exactly one head” is twice as likely as “two heads”.
html.section4_heading: Match the experiment to its number of outcomes
html.worked_example:
Heads and Tails: two fair coins are flipped. Find the probability of getting exactly one head.

1
List every outcome systematically
Put the first coin down the side and the second coin across the top. Each cell is one outcome.
Sample space = {HH, HT, TH, TT}: 4 equally likely outcomes
2
Count the favourable outcomes
Exactly one head happens in HT and in TH: they are different outcomes.
Favourable outcomes = 2
3
Divide and check
P(event) = favourable ÷ total. Check: the four probabilities in the array add to 1.
P(exactly one head) = 24 = 12
html.section6_heading: We do: drawing two team leaders
html.we_do_intro: Five students put their names in a bag: Ana, Ben and Cara are in Year 9, Dev and Eli are in Year 10. Two names are drawn without replacement to be joint team leaders (order does not matter). Grey cells are impossible (the same name twice) or repeats (BA is the same pair as AB).
html.strategy_section:
6bSpot the mistake

A student has answered a Heads and Tails question, but one line of their working is wrong. Click the line where the mistake first appears.

Two fair coins are flipped. Find P(exactly one head).
1Count how many heads show on the two coins.
2The number of heads can be 0, 1 or 2.
3So there are 3 equally likely outcomes: no heads, one head, two heads.
4P(exactly one head) = 1 out of 3 = 13

✓ Right: line 3 is where the reasoning breaks.

Why: 0, 1 and 2 heads are possible results, but they are not equally likely. List the outcomes coin by coin: HH, HT, TH, TT. “One head” happens two ways (HT and TH), so it is twice as likely as “two heads”.

Which is the best rewrite of line 3?

  • A: The equally likely outcomes are HH, HT, TH and TT, so there are 4 outcomes.
  • B: The 3 results are not equally likely, so the probability cannot be found.
  • C: There are only 2 outcomes, heads or tails.

7bHinge check: two dice🎯 Pick one

Before you pick your tier: choose the correct answer. Each wrong option hides a common mistake.

Two fair dice are rolled and the numbers are added. What is P(the sum is 4)?
The sums are not equally likely. A sum of 7 can be made six ways but a sum of 2 only one way. Count cells in the 36-cell array, not possible sums.
Order matters for the outcomes. A 1 on the first die and a 3 on the second is a different cell from a 3 then a 1. You missed (3, 1).
Correct. Three cells of the 6 × 6 array give a sum of 4, so P = 336 = 112.
Multiply, don't add. Each of the 6 results on the first die pairs with each of the 6 on the second: 6 × 6 = 36 outcomes, not 6 + 6 = 12.

retrieval.q: A fair six-sided die is rolled. What is P(rolling a 4)? Type a fraction.
retrieval.hint: One face shows 4 out of six equally likely faces.

retrieval.q: A bag holds 3 red and 5 blue counters. One is drawn at random. What is P(red)?
retrieval.hint: Favourable ÷ total: 3 red out of 3 + 5 counters.

retrieval.q: The probability it rains tomorrow is 0.3. What is the probability it does not rain?
retrieval.hint: The probabilities of an event and its complement add to 1.

practice2.hint: Count the 7s in the array: they run along a diagonal. 6 out of 36.

fb.1/11: There are 11 possible sums, but they are not equally likely. Count cells in the 36-cell array.

practice2.q: Two dice are rolled and added. What is P(sum greater than 9)?
practice2.hint: Sums of 10, 11 or 12: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 cells out of 36.

practice2.q: Four names (Ari, Bea, Cy, Di) are in a bag. Two are drawn without replacement as joint leaders (order does not matter). How many different pairs are possible?
practice2.hint: AB, AC, AD, BC, BD, CD.

fb.12: You have counted AB and BA as different. For joint leaders they are the same pair.
fb.16: Without replacement the same name cannot be drawn twice, and order does not matter.

practice2.q: Using the same four names, what is P(Bea is one of the two leaders)?
practice2.hint: Pairs containing B: AB, BC, BD. 3 out of 6.

fb.1/4: Bea can be drawn first or second: count every pair that contains B.

practice2.q: Now the four names are drawn for captain then vice-captain, so order matters. How many outcomes are possible?
practice2.hint: 4 choices for captain × 3 left for vice-captain.

fb.6: When order matters, Ari-captain/Bea-vice is different from Bea-captain/Ari-vice.
fb.16: Without replacement the captain cannot also be vice-captain: only 3 names are left.

practice2.q: A bag holds 2 red marbles (R₁, R₂) and 1 blue (B). A marble is drawn, replaced, then a second is drawn. What is P(both red)?
practice2.hint: Red-red cells: R₁R₁, R₁R₂, R₂R₁, R₂R₂. 4 out of 9.

fb.1/3: That would be without replacement. Here the first marble goes back, so all 9 cells are possible.

practice3.q: The Heads and Tails stall: a player pays $2, flips two coins and wins $5 for two heads. If 100 games are played, how many wins would you expect?

fb.33: Two heads is 1 outcome of 4, not 1 of 3: HT and TH are separate outcomes.
fb.50: Two heads needs BOTH coins to be heads: 1 outcome out of HH, HT, TH, TT.

practice3.q: For the same 100 games, what profit would the stall expect, in dollars? (Takings minus prize money.)
Six students are nominated: 4 are in Year 9 and 2 are in Year 10. Two are chosen at random as joint leaders. What is P(both are in Year 9)?
practice3.hint: Total pairs: 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15. Year 9 pairs from 4 names: 6. So 6/15.

fb.4/9: That treats the draw as with replacement. A name cannot be chosen twice: list the 15 pairs.

practice3.q: Two dice are rolled and the numbers are multiplied. What is P(the product is even)?
practice3.hint: The product is odd only when both dice are odd: 3 × 3 = 9 cells. Even: 36 − 9 = 27.

fb.1/2: Even × anything is even, so even products are more common than odd ones. Count the odd × odd cells and subtract from 36.

exitProbs.q: Two coins are flipped. What is P(exactly one head)?

fb.1/3: The results 0, 1, 2 heads are not equally likely. List HH, HT, TH, TT.
fb.1/4: Exactly one head happens in HT and in TH: count both.

exitProbs.q: A coin is flipped and a die is rolled. What is P(head and a number greater than 4)?
exitProbs.hint: H5 and H6: 2 cells out of 12.

exitProbs.q: Jo says: “Two coins give three results: two heads, one head, no heads. So P(two heads) = ⅓.” Explain Jo’s mistake.
exitProbs.hint: Are the three results equally likely? Draw the array.
